absent: Numeric values of selectors, flag bits, privilege mask, error numbers, TSS offsets, per CPU offsets, cache line size, entry stack size, ESPFIX sizes and markers.
Full layouts of inactive task frame, task struct thread fields, TSS, trap frame, entry stack, ESPFIX stacks, and per CPU area.
Definitions and side effects of save and restore and table switch and buffer clear and return buffer fill and branch mitigation and leak erasure and frame encode and unwind macros.

Contracts and return conventions of high level handlers for SYSENTER and INT80 and 64 bit system call and NMI and fork return and context switch and double fault shim and Xen upcall and general protection.
Locking and interrupt disable nesting and preemption rules beyond disabled IRQs on 64 bit entry and flag sanitization before preemption on SYSENTER.
Page table isolation and Xen PV and FRED and ESPFIX configuration effects beyond the alternative branches shown.
VDSO SYSEXIT resume protocol and user register expectations after fast returns.

findings.text: The 32 bit entry layer publishes global code symbols for low level context switch and fork return and SYSENTER dispatch and INT80 dispatch and generic exception dispatch and double fault gate and NMI gate so that vector tables and C code can transfer control to them.

The 64 bit entry layer and shared trap helper publish global code and data symbols for 64 bit system call entry and low level context switch and fork return and Xen error entry and common interrupt return hub and GS loader and Xen hypervisor callback and Xen failsafe callback plus a warning trap stub and a segment selector word.

SYSENTER 32 entry starts on the entry stack with live user registers, preserves flags and syscall number across a switch to kernel address tables, moves to the task stack through a TSS mapping, builds a kernel trap frame with placeholders for user stack pointer and user instruction pointer, saves remaining user state, sanitizes sensitive flag bits, then calls the high level SYSENTER dispatcher and either takes a slow exit or attempts an opportunistic SYSEXIT fast return.

INT80 32 entry suppresses user access, records the incoming syscall number, saves full user state with stack switching, calls the high level INT80 dispatcher, then falls into a shared restore sequence that erases kernel stack leaks, returns to the entry stack, applies ESPFIX, switches to user address tables, restores user registers and returns with IRET plus a fault fixup that diverts IRET faults to the exception path.

SYSCALL 64 entry swaps GS, stashes the user stack pointer in TSS scratch space, switches to kernel address tables and to the top of the kernel stack, constructs a trap frame holding user segments and stack and flags and return address and syscall number, saves and clears general registers, normalizes the syscall number as signed 32 bit, applies speculation mitigations, then calls the 64 bit system call dispatcher with interrupts disabled and selects fast SYSRET return or the slow common return.

The 32 bit generic exception trampoline saves full state with stack switching and frame encoding while skipping GS, fetches the handler address from the GS slot of the frame, marks the frame as not a restartable system call while preserving the hardware error code locally, invokes the handler indirectly with a trap frame pointer, then branches to user or kernel return based on saved privilege.

The 32 bit NMI gate suppresses user access, detects entry from the ESPFIX stack and from the SYSENTER stack, saves state with an NMI safe sequence, passes a zero error code plus trap frame pointer to the high level NMI handler, bounces through the thread stack when found on the SYSENTER stack, then performs NMI safe restore with ESPFIX handling and CPU buffer clearing before jumping to the shared IRET label.

The 32 bit double fault gate is a task gate handler that assumes an otherwise empty stack, clears the task switched flag and the nested task flag, delegates to a double fault shim helper, never attempts IRET return, and parks the CPU in a halt loop; it intentionally ignores the always zero error code for robustness against hypervisor quirks.

The 64 bit common interrupt return hub provides user return and kernel return paths with alternatives for Xen PV and page table isolation trampoline and 64 bit ESPFIX for LDT stack segments, performs privilege assertions before IRET, copies the IRET frame to a trampoline stack when isolation is active, and centralizes mitigations such as indirect branch control exit and stack leak erasure and CPU buffer clearing.

The low level 32 bit and 64 bit context switch trampolines save callee preserved registers, exchange the kernel stack pointer between outgoing and incoming tasks through per task saved stack fields, refresh the stack guard from the incoming task when the protector is enabled, refresh return prediction state when the relevant CPU feature is present, restore the incoming register set, and tail call the generic context switch routine.

The 32 bit and 64 bit fork return trampolines act as the first kernel execution of a new task, supplying previous task plus trap frame plus start function plus start argument to the generic fork return helper, with the 32 bit form pushing an unwind return address and cleaning its argument slot and the 64 bit form marking end of stack and unwind register state before jumping to the user return path with a FRED alternative when enabled.

Xen 64 bit helpers include an error entry that saves and clears registers while preserving the return address and mitigating return prediction before returning, a hypervisor callback that adopts its incoming pointer as stack pointer because it never returns and then invokes the event channel upcall handler before diverting to error return, and a failsafe callback that classifies IRET versus segment failures.

The GS loader attempts to install a caller supplied index into GS while swapped to kernel GS, enforces ordering for a swap GS erratum, and on fault returns to user GS, optionally sanitizes a null segment condition, clears GS and retries through an exception table relation; the warning trap stub raises a faulting undefined instruction using a memory operand and an argument register then returns.

Task and CPU state accessed by entry code includes a per task saved kernel stack pointer used to exchange stacks, a per task stack canary copied into the per CPU guard on switch, TSS fields mapping the entry stack to the task stack and supplying entry and scratch stack pointers, plus per CPU current stack top and entry area base and translation base used to detect SYSENTER stack residence and to select return stacks.

Trap frames built on the kernel stack carry user stack segment and stack pointer and flags and code segment and instruction pointer plus original syscall number defaulted to a negated no syscall error, with SYSENTER using placeholders for stack pointer and instruction pointer later completed by other logic; the 64 bit LDT return uses an eight slot per CPU ESPFIX area holding user AX and IP and CS and flags and SP and SS with read only aliases keyed by high bits of user SP.

Callee preserved register save and restore order in both context switch trampolines must correspond to the inactive task frame layout; the 32 bit form additionally saves and restores flags around the switch to avoid leaking the alignment check state to the next task.

SYSENTER must clear nested task and alignment check and trap flag state before enabling preemption, using a fast test with an out of line fixed flags restore for the uncommon set case; single step through the entry region is tolerated by letting debug ignore traps up to the end of region marker.

Entries that arrive on the entry stack switch from user to kernel address tables early using a scratch register while preserving live user values, and exits switch back to user tables late on a trampoline or entry stack; several paths assert the expected table base before IRET or POPF style restoration and fault if the check fails.

Return target after a 32 bit exception is decided from saved privilege: with virtual 8086 support the decision combines flags VM bit and code segment privilege, otherwise it uses code segment privilege alone; user and virtual 8086 targets use the shared user restore path while kernel targets use a paranoid kernel exit with table verification and direct register restore.

NMI entry must not trust the interrupted stack: presence on the SYSENTER entry stack is detected by range comparison against the per CPU entry area and handled by temporarily running on the thread stack and then restoring the entry stack pointer, while ESPFIX entry and return use distinct save and LSS restore sequences keyed by markers in the saved code segment.

Speculation and data leak controls are integral to entry and exit: return buffer filling on context switch when the context switch feature is present, indirect branch control entry and exit around 64 bit system calls and returns, return un-training and branch history clearing on 64 bit entry, CPU buffer clearing before IRET or SYSRET or SYSEXIT style returns, user access suppression on 32 bit entries, and kernel stack leak erasure on exits.

SYSENTER dispatch has two completions selected by the high level handler result: a slow completion falling into the shared INT80 restore and IRET path, or an opportunistic SYSEXIT completion that stages flags and result on the entry stack, restores user registers and FS with a fixup that clears FS on fault, moves to the entry stack, switches tables, restores flags with deferred interrupt enable, and exits with SYSEXIT back to VDSO.

SYSCALL 64 completion has a fast SYSRET path only for a clean 64 bit user context and otherwise uses the slow common return; Xen PV forces the slow path, page table isolation inserts a trampoline IRET frame copy plus table switch, debug builds assert user versus kernel mode before IRET, and fork return selects normal versus FRED user exit by alternative patching.

Fault and callback returns distinguish recoverable IRET faults from fatal ones: IRET failure on 32 bit user return synthesizes a zero error frame and enters the exception dispatcher, 64 bit LDT stack segment returns detour through the ESPFIX alias stack before IRET, Xen failsafe treats matching saved segments as a bad IRET diverted to general protection handling and mismatched segments as a retryable bad segment diverted to error return with a non syscall marker.

Entry hazards addressed in the fragments include return predictor entries containing user addresses across privilege or task changes, alignment check leakage through flags, stale CPU buffers on return to user, kernel stack content leakage on exit, wrong address tables at IRET, faults on the IRET instruction itself, loss of the prior address base after a task gate double fault, faults while loading GS, and reentrancy of NMI over SYSENTER and ESPFIX stacks.

Segment and alignment constants relied upon include a kernel data selector stored as a word in executable space aligned to the L1 cache line size with trap fill, plus user code and user data selectors used when constructing trap frames and when sanitizing GS, and an ESPFIX stack segment value used to recognize NMI arrival on the fixup stack.

Control constants relied upon include flag bits for nested task and alignment check and trap and interrupt and fixed image and virtual 8086 mode, a code privilege mask with a user privilege value, a negated no syscall error used as the default original register and a minus one marker for non system call frames, plus TSS and entry stack and per CPU offsets and ESPFIX code markers used to select save and restore variants.
